en: The Compendium of Right Practice, composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Qingjue of Baoying Monastery in the Western Capital.
Generally speaking, a gentleman does not depend on nobility, nor on meanness; he does not depend on poverty, nor on wealth.
It depends solely upon practice. The constitution of a gentleman is perfected through virtuous conduct and augmented by filial piety and reverence.
Therefore, his breadth, stability, integrity, and purity are such that the world cannot attain them. His breadth is like the ocean; his stability is like a mountain;
his integrity is like the pine tree; his purity is like water. That which is as broad as the ocean is deep beyond measure and vast beyond limit.
It is unfathomable. Deplete it and it does not fall; add to it and it does not overflow. Stir it and you cannot make it turbid;
defile it and you cannot alter its clarity. It is as if hidden within a pearl or harboring a treasure; vast and boundless, there is nothing it does not contain.
That which is as solid as a mountain is lofty yet not precarious, enduring for long without decaying; it cannot be moved by shifting it, nor can it be tilted by shaking it.
Seclusion and stillness cannot cause it to cease its existence, nor can dust and grime combine with it to obscure it.

Thus, whether hidden among the worthy or concealed among the immortals, in rugged terrains or vast distances, there is nowhere it does not grow. That which is as steadfast as a pine knows nothing of flourishing or withering.
Evergreen and enduring, frost and snow cannot cause it to wither; winter and summer cannot alter its hue.
Like the purity of water—whether of the Ji or Wei rivers—it is naturally tranquil and serene. As a mirror, it cannot conceal the forms of things;
as a lubricant, nothing can surpass its utility. Thus, the true gentleman possesses a broad and magnanimous capacity, lofty discernment, and far-reaching vision, thereby cultivating his own nature.

Quiet their spirit, cultivate their virtue, and accumulate their conduct, thereby providing instruction and continuity. Be neither licentious nor wanton; do not insult others nor be arrogant. Sever both slander and praise;
do not expose the faults of others, nor practice your own transgressions. Harmonize your light and blend with the dust of the world.
Recommend the worthy and entrust them with their duties. Be reverent in every ritual and compliant in every task. This is filial piety.
There is nothing he does not accord with; his righteousness is without lack of loyalty. He embodies and examines wisdom, discerning between the worthy and the foolish.
He does not allow excessive seeking to disturb his mind; he does not allow greed or violence to harm himself; he does not take delight in calamity despite being submerged in it like mud and fire;

and he does not abandon the old to pursue the new. Therefore, he entrusts himself to the Way and maintains vast magnanimity; he always fortifies his heart and guards his resolve. These four qualities constitute a Great Man.
This is the essential way of the noble person (*jūnin*). Furthermore, one’s conduct must be like the sun and moon; one’s capacity must be like the mountains and rivers;

one must accord with the four seasons; and one must harmonize with the myriad things. To have conduct like the sun and moon means to ensure that there is no partial illumination. To have a capacity like the mountains and rivers means to ensure that there is no change or alteration.
To accord with the four seasons means to ensure that there is regularity and reliability. To harmonize with the myriad things means to enable them to understand movement and stillness.
Therefore it is said: When a gentleman possesses virtue, the four quarters praise him; when a provincial governor possesses virtue, the common people revere him;
when a village elder possesses virtue, the multitude looks up to him; when a patriarch of the family possesses virtue, the family tradition becomes illustrious.
Heaven has no partiality; it assists only virtue. It is like a *páng* weed growing amidst hemp—it stands straight of its own accord without being propped up. Like...
The orchid mingles among clusters of fragrant flowers; it is naturally perfumed without waiting for incense. It does not harm others to benefit itself;
it does not consider itself right because others are wrong. It does not exalt itself by disparaging others, nor does it value itself by belittling others.
It does not form friendships through unrighteous means, nor does it harbor enmity toward those who have caused resentment. It does not covet wealth that lacks moral justification. It does not...
One receives rewards for no merit; one bestows kindness without expecting a return, yet when a return is made, one regrets it is not more profound.
Thus, the Book says: "If confronted with wealth, his integrity is seen; if approached with beauty, his constancy is seen; if warned of danger—"
Thus, one observes their courage. By intoxicating them with wine, one observes their true character. Zhuangzi said: "Send them on distant missions to observe their loyalty;
employ them in tasks nearby to observe their respectfulness; entrust them with difficult tasks to observe their capability;

question them at the end of a matter to observe their wisdom; impose urgent deadlines to observe their reliability; and observe those who have received honors and rank to see if they are arrogant or extravagant. Regarding glory...
In others, one observes their lack of boastfulness; in the young, their reverence; in those fond of learning, their integrity and dedication to practice;
in the elderly, their circumspection and refusal to transgress; and between fathers and sons, their mutual affection and filial piety.
Among brothers, one observes their mutual friendship; among neighbors, one observes their integrity and trustworthiness; between ruler and subject, one observes their loyalty and benevolence.

Therefore, one must be cautious at the beginning and protect against the end, refining one's reputation and sharpening one's conduct, so that neither the depraved nor the upright shall alter their heart.
If one repeatedly returns to the path without altering their resolve, governing subordinates with leniency and occupying a high position without arrogance,
then such a person may be considered material for broad cultivation and will forever be free from fault and blemish.
Forty-eight [deities] and so forth.
The sage emulates Heaven and follows Earth; the worthy person dwells in the profound and unfathomable;
the person of the Way has no obstruction in the mind; the awakened person knows their own original nature.
The person of relinquishment knows how to bestow without attachment; the person of ethical discipline examines both transgressions and blessings;
the person of patience has no faults in their speech; the person of diligence cultivates practice without indolence;
the person of concentration has no mental distraction; the person of wisdom remains far removed from worldly guile and artifice.
The righteous man dedicates merit and yields virtue; he examines the hearing and sight of others and does not find fault with their governance.
He follows the public way and is not private; he scrutinizes the non-virtue of others and does not accept wealth.
He brings peace to the hearts of men so they have no divergent movements; he hides himself and withdraws from the world to nurture his virtue.
He is reverent toward people, never failing in ritual propriety; he respects his superiors and loves those below him.
He is trustworthy toward people, his word never being double-faceted. He is cautious toward people, never overstepping ritual bounds;
he is generous toward people and those under his authority, never treating them with peril. He is profound toward people, possessing foresight regarding what has not yet sprouted.
The virtuous person does not harbor anger in their inner conduct;
the practitioner delights in recounting good deeds and plans for others with deep knowledge and far-reaching vision;

the loyal official serves his sovereign to the utmost of his integrity, yielding to others while recommending the worthy and employing the capable; the thrifty person exercises moderation in expenditure and avoids waste.
Filial persons serve their elders without fail; wise persons do not dwell in darkness;
discerning persons do not accept idle words; students draw near to spiritual friends;
compassionate persons harbor no intent to kill; and wealthy persons relieve the poor and bestow gifts upon others.
Noble people revere the Buddha and honor the Sangha; Enlightened people do not covet the five desires;
Pure people are untainted by worldly dust; Serenely-minded people awaken their intent and know emptiness;
Great-hearted people encompass heaven and earth; Good people promote the virtuous and recommend the worthy.
The fool knows not shame; the deluded man does not reflect upon the worthy and virtuous;
the obstinate man fears not the public law; the wicked man always delights in taking life;
the turbid man cannot distinguish between the clear and the defiled; the worldly man covets wealth and clings to sensual desires.
Those who oppose righteousness are unfilial toward their parents; petty people do not recognize the distinction between the honorable and the humble.
For a gentleman who establishes himself as a person, there is nothing that exceeds these forty-eight grades.

However, if one aligns their being with the Great Way, they belong to the rank of sages and worthies. If filial piety is not practiced within the family and compassion is not practiced within oneself, [one cannot attain this].
Kindness was not shown to one's kin; favors did not reach others; righteousness was not bestowed upon friends; loyalty was not extended to the state; valor did not save those in peril;
counsel was not trusted by the virtuous; magnanimity was not displayed toward subordinates; and clarity was not exercised in examining affairs.
To treat one who is not a kinsman as a kinsman is flattery; to treat a kinsman who is poor with neglect is perversity.

To turn one’s back on the good and incline toward the evil, to plot the ruin of the loyal and virtuous, and to attach oneself to petty men while keeping distance from gentlemen—these are things that Heaven will not tolerate;
what need is there to speak further of them? The worthy revere virtue, while the foolish prize wealth. As for those adorned with fine silks and flowery ornaments:
One who wears fine silken robes must know those who wear plain cloth; one who partakes of delicacies and jade-like food must know those who eat dregs and husks;

one who dwells in carved walls and lofty mansions must know those who live in thatched huts; one who has accumulated a thousand measures of grain must know those who have but a peck or a pint in store;
one who holds high office and great rank must know the harm of grievous injustice; and one who dwells in peace and joy must know [the suffering of the displaced].

One must know that there is the toil of being driven and employed; one who leaps upon a horse and brandishes a whip must know the suffering of bearing burdens. When people are in peril, distress, or urgent difficulty, one ought to rescue them; one must not sit idly by and watch their fate unfold. Those who see danger and do not come to the rescue— [The text continues: ...are as those who, seeing a fire raging on a mountain, do not extinguish it with water; they are as those who, seeing a person drowning in a river, do not pull them out with their hands; they are as those who, seeing a tree about to fall, do not brace it with a supporting beam; they are as those who, seeing a boat about to sink, do not bail out the water with a ladle; they are as those who, seeing a house about to collapse, do not prop it up with a pillar; they are as those who, seeing a wall about to crumble, do not reinforce it with a buttress; they are as those who, seeing a bridge about to break, do not mend it with timber; they are as those who, seeing a path about to be blocked, do not clear it with a hoe; they are as those who, seeing a well about to run dry, do not draw water from it with a bucket; they are as those who, seeing a field about to be parched, do not irrigate it with a canal; they are as those who, seeing a pond about to dry up, do not scoop out the mud with a shovel; they are as those who, seeing a garden about to wither, do not water it with a watering can; they are as those who, seeing a tree about to die, do not nourish it with manure; they are as those who, seeing a child about to starve, do not feed it with milk; they are as those who, seeing a sick person about to perish, do not administer medicine; they are as those who, seeing a hungry person about to die, do not offer food; they are as those who, seeing a cold person about to freeze, do not provide clothing; they are as those who, seeing a thirsty person about to die, do not give drink; they are as those who, seeing a weary person about to collapse, do not offer rest; they are as those who, seeing a burdened person about to falter, do not lend a hand; they are as those who, seeing a person in grief about to weep, do not offer comfort; they are as those who, seeing a person in fear about to tremble, do not grant protection; they are as those who, seeing a person in anger about to strike, do not restrain them; they are as those who, seeing a person in delusion about to err, do not guide them; they are as those who, seeing a person in doubt about to wander, do not show the way; they are as those who, seeing a person in sorrow about to lament, do not console them; they are as those who, seeing a person in pain about to cry out, do not soothe them; they are as those who, seeing a person in exhaustion about to faint, do not revive them; they are as those who, seeing a person in despair about to lose hope, do not encourage them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to perish, do not save them; they are as those who, seeing a person in calamity about to die, do not assist them; they are as those who, seeing a person in misfortune about to fall, do not support them; they are as those who, seeing a person in adversity about to sink, do not lift them up; they are as those who, seeing a person in decline about to vanish, do not preserve them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be lost, do not restore them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be destroyed, do not rebuild them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be annihilated, do not revive them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be obliterated, do not resurrect them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be extinguished, do not rekindle them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be ended, do not renew them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be finished, do not complete them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be concluded, do not conclude for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be finalized, do not finalize for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be settled, do not settle for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be resolved, do not resolve for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be determined, do not determine for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be decided, do not decide for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be fixed, do not fix for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be established, do not establish for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be confirmed, do not confirm for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be validated, do not validate for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be proven, do not prove for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be certified, do not certify for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be authenticated, do not authenticate for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be verified, do not verify for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be attested, do not attest for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be testified, do not testify for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be sworn, do not swear for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be bound, do not bind for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be fettered, do not fetter for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be shackled, do not shackle for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be imprisoned, do not imprison for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be confined, do not confine for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be locked up, do not lock up for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be secured, do not secure for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be guarded, do not guard for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be protected, do not protect for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be shielded, do not shield for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be defended, do not defend for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be saved, do not save for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be rescued, do not rescue for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be delivered, do not deliver for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be liberated, do not liberate for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be freed, do not free for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be released, do not release for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be let go, do not let go for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be dismissed, do not dismiss for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be sent away, do not send away for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be banished, do not banish for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be expelled, do not expel for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be cast out, do not cast out for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be abandoned, do not abandon for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be forsaken, do not forsake for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be left behind, do not leave behind for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be excluded, do not exclude for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be separated, do not separate for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be parted, do not part for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be divided, do not divide for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to be severed, do not sever for them; they are as those who, seeing a person in ruin about to
One who does not know contentment is no human being. One who sees poverty and does not provide relief is no human being. One who bestows kindness while expecting a reward is no human being.
One who does not reform their own faults is no human being. One who treats superiors with contempt and acts arrogantly toward inferiors is no human being.
One who deceives the noble for the sake of the lowly is not human. One who takes bribes and harms others is not human.
One who surrenders public affairs to private interests is not human. One who is unfilial toward one’s parents is not human. One who is unfriendly toward one’s brothers is not human.
One who is not a human being is one who does not harmonize with their six kin; one who is not a human being is one who does not delight in good deeds.
Indeed, a person must comprehend the Three Powers, cherish the Six Arts, set their will upon the four quarters, possess the five beauties, sever the four evils, and eliminate the three delusions.
Contemplate the nine fears and recognize the four anxieties. Do not sleep excessively. Practice *tai-xi* (embryonic breathing). Be cautious in speech and moderate in eating and drinking;
these are the foundations for being careful of one's person and frugal in expenditure. Furthermore, one must establish those four gates to achieve complete excellence:

serve the sovereign by establishing the gate of loyalty; serve one’s parents by establishing the gate of filial piety; serve friends by establishing the gate of righteousness; and serve teachers and elders by establishing the gate of reverence.
The Gate of Loyalty refers to sacrificing one's life when facing peril. The Gate of Filial Piety refers to nourishing one's parents with a respectful countenance and practicing reverence.
The Gate of Righteousness refers to having a mind that never wavers or changes. The Gate of Prudence refers to being free from all indolence.
The doctrines of the Three Teachings share one and the same meaning.
In Confucianism, benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, wisdom, and sincerity are all directed toward loyalty and filial piety toward sovereign and father.
In Buddhism, compassion and the salvation from suffering are directed toward the transformation and guidance of the deluded masses.
As for Daoism, it is characterized by silence and tranquility, returning to a state of non-greed and non-attachment.
Therefore, the teachings of the Three Teachings may be upheld and revered.

By investigating and scrutinizing them, once their subtleties are penetrated and their origins understood, one will naturally attain the Way of the sages and worthies, as well as the conduct of the virtuous and the noble. It is thus.
If one assists the state, why worry that yin and yang will not be harmonious, wind and rain will not be timely, the common people will not be at peace, or the populace will not be prosperous?
If one governs the family, why worry that brothers will not be cordial, the six kin will not be harmonious, or rites and music will not be practiced?
The preceding and succeeding sections were not properly arranged; I have compiled this collection. I dare not delve deeply into its meaning or embellish its phrasing.
What I value is its ability to guide the blind masses and be transmitted to future generations. Since words alone are insufficient, I have composed this eulogy to further express it.

The eulogy says: How magnificent is the gentleman! He practices only that which is good; he maintains loyalty and filial piety. His desires are unknown, and his conduct does not transgress the Classics;
his speech does not exceed the Histories. Serene and silent, dignified and upright, he provides a lofty guidance toward profound principles.

Turning toward the good and turning away from evil, Opening one’s heart to seek the principle; If poor, finding joy within oneself, And if wealthy, likewise cherishing righteousness— Alas for such a person!
Truly, they are not easily found.
The Collection of Right Practice (Concluded).
The Abbot of the Baiyun School (Your Servant) Monk Mingren,
having received the official dispatch from the Directorate for the Supervision of All Meritorious Works on the twenty-eighth day of the tenth month of the first year of Huangqing,
[records that] it was the first day of Bayu’s *qeshig*.
Within the Jiaxi Hall, at one time, Sugurichana Huaiqie Limachi, Boluochaer, Tongzhi Guanyin Nu, and others came;
there were also officials from this office, including the Grand Minister of State and Director of the Bureau of Merit Nianzhen Qulasier,
and the Vice Director of the Bureau of Merit Zhang.
He dispatched Aliya Dasi to respectfully deliver the imperial decree regarding the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vidhi* and the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-pūjā-vidhi* translated by Sarapa. Furthermore, Baiyun...
The *Record of the Master’s Initial Studies* was submitted by you with official documents to the Jiangzhe Provincial Government.
Once the Baiyun sect had finished carving the woodblocks and printing it, did you not submit it to be included within the Tripitaka?
So it is said.
The Imperial Decree has been received. Having respectfully received this, the Zhongshu Sheng (Central Secretariat) has issued a formal notification for execution.
In accordance with the Imperial Command, it has been dispatched to all circuits.

This humble monk Mingren, with the utmost reverence for this gracious mandate, has commissioned artisans at Daci Yin Temple to carve the woodblocks for printing, so that it may be respectfully included in the Tripitaka.

Circulated for wide distribution. The vast causes thus accumulated are solely to pray for the Emperor’s ten-thousand-fold longevity and for the Empress Dowager’s sagacious years to equal those of Heaven.
May the Empress live for ten thousand years;
may the Crown Prince and all the princes live for a thousand autumns; may the civil and military officials always retain their ranks and emoluments;
and we further pray that the state shall be prosperous and the people at peace, with timely rains and sunshine.
The Buddha-sun increases in brilliance; the Wheel of Dharma turns eternally.
On the [blank] day of the fourth month in the second year of Huangqing, the monk (Mingren), your servant, respectfully inscribes this.
